title: Hierarchical Inheritance
summary: Master hierarchical inheritance in Java: how one common superclass is extended by multiple sibling subclasses, ensuring isolated specialization.
learningObjectives: Understand the architecture of hierarchical inheritance (one parent, multiple siblings)
Verify complete isolation between sibling subclasses (Sibling A cannot access Sibling B's members)
Distinguish when to extend an existing parent versus creating a new sibling
Model real-world polymorphic sibling structures (e.g. Shape -> Circle, Rectangle, Triangle)
expectedOutcomes: Ability to design robust sibling hierarchies branching from a common enterprise base class
Understanding sibling isolation rules in compile-time type checking

activities.title: The Universal Vehicle Blueprint in an Automobile Factory
activities.content:
Imagine an automotive manufacturing plant with a master chassis blueprint: the **MotorVehicle Blueprint**.

From this single blueprint, the factory branches into three separate assembly lines:
1. **The Sedan Assembly Line**: adds family seating and a trunk.
2. **The Pickup Truck Assembly Line**: adds an open flatbed and heavy-duty towing.
3. **The Ambulance Assembly Line**: adds emergency sirens and medical life-support beds.

All three share the identical core motor, steering, and braking engineering from the MotorVehicle parent blueprint. But a Sedan has zero knowledge of an Ambulance siren, and a Truck has zero access to a Sedan trunk. They are independent sibling specializations.

activities.title: Architecture, Branching, and Strict Sibling Isolation
activities.content:
Hierarchical inheritance occurs when **two or more classes extend the same superclass**.

```
                    +-------------------+
                    |      Account      | (Superclass)
                    +-------------------+
                              ^
                              |
               +--------------+--------------+
               |                             |
     +-------------------+         +-------------------+
     |  SavingsAccount   |         |  CheckingAccount  | (Siblings)
     +-------------------+         +-------------------+
```

### 1. Architectural Traits:
- **One Shared Superclass**: Common fields (`accountNumber`, `balance`) and methods (`deposit()`, `getBalance()`) are centralized.
- **Multiple Subclasses**: Each subclass introduces its own specialized fields and operations.

### 2. Strict Sibling Isolation (Crucial Interview Concept!):
- **Siblings do NOT know about each other**: `SavingsAccount` has no access to fields or methods declared in `CheckingAccount`.
- You **cannot assign** an instance of `SavingsAccount` to a variable of type `CheckingAccount` (they are in completely separate branches of the inheritance tree).

### 3. Core Rules:
- A superclass is extended by multiple subclasses (`class Dog extends Animal`, `class Cat extends Animal`).
- Every sibling has independent heap memory and independent runtime state.
- Changes to the shared superclass propagate to all siblings automatically.

activities.title: Bank Account Sibling Hierarchy: Savings vs Checking
activities.description: Trace how SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount inherit shared balance logic while keeping specializations isolated.

steps.description: BankAccount centralizes common state: accountId and balance.
SavingsAccount specializes with interestRate and addInterest().
CheckingAccount specializes with feePerCheck and writeCheck().
Notice sibling isolation: SavingsAccount cannot call writeCheck(), and CheckingAccount cannot call addInterest().

activities.title: Example 2: Employee -> Developer and Manager
activities.description: Witness sibling branching in corporate role modeling.

steps.description: Developer and Manager share Employee's name and salary.
Each sibling implements distinct specialized operations independently.

questions.question: What is hierarchical inheritance in Java?
options: A class having multiple parent classes
Multiple subclasses extending the same single superclass
A class having no superclasses except Object
An interface extending multiple interfaces
questions.explanation: Hierarchical inheritance occurs when one superclass is extended by two or more sibling subclasses.

questions.question: If Dog and Cat both extend Animal, can a Dog object access Cat's meow() method?
options: Yes, because they share the same parent Animal
No, sibling classes are completely isolated and have no access to each other's members
Yes, using the sibling keyword
Only if meow() is marked protected
questions.explanation: Sibling classes are completely isolated. Subclass members are not shared horizontally across siblings.

questions.question: What happens if a developer attempts: 'CheckingAccount chk = new SavingsAccount("S1", 100);' where both extend BankAccount?
options: It compiles and runs normally
Compile-time error: Incompatible types (SavingsAccount cannot be converted to CheckingAccount)
The JVM converts interest into check fees automatically
Runtime SiblingCastException
questions.explanation: Siblings are unrelated types in the type system. You cannot assign one sibling reference to another.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of hierarchical inheritance?
options: It allows a class to have multiple parents
It centralizes common logic in a single parent while enabling diverse, specialized child classes
It eliminates all need for constructors
It makes memory allocation zero-cost
questions.explanation: It promotes code reuse across multiple specialized classes derived from one common base.

questions.question: If a bug is discovered in the shared superclass of 8 sibling classes, how many files must be patched?
options: All 8 sibling files must be patched
Only the single superclass file needs to be patched
The JVM patch tool must be run
Each sibling must be deleted and regenerated
questions.explanation: Centralizing shared logic in the superclass ensures fixing the bug once repairs all 8 siblings automatically.

questions.question: Can two sibling classes declare methods with the exact same name and signature?
options: No, that causes a duplicate method compilation error
Yes, each sibling is an independent scope and can declare identical method names without conflict
Only if the superclass declares the method first
Only if one of them is private
questions.explanation: Because sibling classes are independent class scopes, they can each declare methods with identical names.

questions.question: In Java's standard library, java.lang.Number is extended by Integer, Double, Long, and Float. What kind of inheritance is this?
options: Multiple inheritance
Hierarchical inheritance
Cyclic inheritance
Diamond inheritance
questions.explanation: Multiple sibling classes (Integer, Double, Long) extending a single parent (Number) is a classic example of hierarchical inheritance.

questions.question: Can a sibling class override a method inherited from the common superclass without affecting other siblings?
options: No, changing one sibling changes all siblings
Yes, any method customization in one sibling applies only to instances of that specific sibling class
Only if the superclass method is static
Only if the parent class is final
questions.explanation: Modifications or specialized methods in a child class affect only instances of that child class.

questions.question: Which relationship best models hierarchical inheritance?
options: A horizontal linear sequence
A branching tree with one root node branching into multiple leaf nodes
A bidirectional graph with cycles
An inverted pyramid
questions.explanation: Hierarchical inheritance models a branching tree: one root parent branching into multiple child branches.

questions.question: Can an instance of a sibling class access private variables of the shared superclass?
options: Yes, because all siblings share them
No, private variables are accessible only within the superclass itself
Only if the sibling is created in the same file
Only if the sibling calls super.getPrivate()
questions.explanation: Private variables in the superclass remain private and cannot be directly accessed by any subclass or sibling.

interviewQA.question: What is hierarchical inheritance and how does it differ from multiple inheritance?
interviewQA.answer: Hierarchical inheritance is 'one parent -> multiple children' (e.g. Animal extended by Dog and Cat). Multiple inheritance is 'multiple parents -> one child' (e.g. Child extending ParentA and ParentB). Java fully supports hierarchical inheritance, but prohibits multiple class inheritance.

interviewQA.question: Explain sibling isolation in Java's type system.
interviewQA.answer: Sibling isolation means two classes that share a common superclass have zero relationship with one another horizontally. Sibling A cannot call methods or access fields declared exclusively in Sibling B, and references of type Sibling A cannot hold instances of Sibling B.

interviewQA.question: Give an example of hierarchical inheritance from the Java standard library.
interviewQA.answer: java.lang.Throwable is the superclass of Exception and Error. java.lang.Number is the superclass of Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, and Double. java.io.InputStream is the superclass of FileInputStream, ByteArrayInputStream, and BufferedInputStream.

interviewQA.question: How do you decide whether to create a new sibling subclass vs modifying an existing class?
interviewQA.answer: If a new requirement represents a distinct specialization with unique fields, validation rules, or business operations that do not apply to other siblings (e.g. adding FixedDepositAccount alongside SavingsAccount), create a new sibling subclass. This adheres to the Open-Closed Principle.

interviewQA.question: Can sibling classes share code between each other without pushing it to the superclass?
interviewQA.answer: If shared code is placed in one sibling, other siblings cannot reach it. To share logic cleanly without cluttering the parent, engineers either move the common logic up to the superclass (if it applies to all siblings), create an intermediate subclass, or extract the logic into a composed helper utility.

interviewQA.question: What is the memory layout difference between two instances of different sibling classes?
interviewQA.answer: Both instances allocate memory for the superclass fields (e.g. balance, accountId), but each instance allocates additional memory only for its own specialized fields (e.g. SavingsAccount allocates interestRate, while CheckingAccount allocates overdraftFee).

activities.title: Module 5 Lesson 6 Mastery Checkpoint
checklist: I understand the architecture of hierarchical inheritance (one parent, multiple children)
I understand strict sibling isolation (no horizontal field or method access between siblings)
I know why assigning one sibling reference to another sibling type fails compilation
I can cite standard library examples (Number -> Integer, Double; Throwable -> Exception, Error)
I understand how shared superclass bug fixes propagate to all sibling subclasses
I know that siblings can declare methods with identical names without collision
I understand the memory footprint of sibling instances
I know when to extract shared logic into the superclass vs keeping it in a sibling
I can design a branching sibling class tree in Java
I can implement a working 3-sibling banking or notification system

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Shape Superclass with Circle and Rectangle Siblings
practiceProblems.description: Create a Shape superclass extended by Circle and Rectangle sibling subclasses.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement Shape with color (String). Create sibling Circle adding radius (double) and printArea(). Create sibling Rectangle adding width (double), height (double) and printArea().
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Red Circle area: 78.53981633974483
Blue Rectangle area: 40.0
hints: printArea() in Rectangle computes width * height.

practiceProblems.title: Code from Scratch: Notification Sibling Hierarchy (Email & SMS)
practiceProblems.description: Construct Notification parent class and EmailNotification / SmsNotification sibling subclasses.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Build Notification with recipient (String) and message (String). Create sibling EmailNotification adding subject (String) and sendEmail(). Create sibling SmsNotification adding characterLimit (int) and sendSms(). From scratch.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Sending Email to user@domain.com [Subject: Security Alert]: Password reset requested
Sending SMS to +15550199 (Max 160 chars): Your verification code is 4491
hints: Notification constructor initializes recipient and message.
EmailNotification and SmsNotification each call super(recipient, message).
Print formatted output matching test expectations.

practiceProblems.title: Code from Scratch: Bank Account Branching with FixedDeposit and CurrentAccount
practiceProblems.description: Construct Account superclass with FixedDeposit and CurrentAccount siblings with distinct penalties.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create Account with accountNum (String), balance (double). Create sibling FixedDeposit adding tenureMonths (int) and prematureWithdrawalPenalty (double). Create sibling CurrentAccount adding overdraftLimit (double) and checkLimit(). From scratch.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
FD Account FD-10 balance: $50000.0 (Penalty for early exit: 2.5%)
Current Account CA-20 balance: $12000.0 (Overdraft: $5000.0)
hints: FixedDeposit and CurrentAccount extend Account independently.
Write displayInfo() in each sibling printing their respective terms.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Broken Code: Attempted Cross-Sibling Method Call
practiceProblems.description: Fix a compilation failure caused by calling a sibling-specific method on another sibling.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: In the code, a client attempts to call Dog's bark() method on a Cat instance. Fix the code so both Dog and Cat execute their own respective sibling methods.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Rover barks: Woof!
Whiskers meows: Meow!
hints: Siblings do not share methods declared in sibling subclasses.

practiceProblems.title: Challenge: Multi-Channel Cloud Storage Providers
practiceProblems.description: Design CloudBucket superclass with S3Bucket, GcsBucket, and AzureBlobBucket sibling subclasses.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create CloudBucket with bucketName (String), region (String), storageClass (String). Create sibling S3Bucket adding versioningEnabled (boolean). Create sibling GcsBucket adding retentionPeriodDays (int). Create sibling AzureBlobBucket adding accessTier (String). Implement displaySpecs() on all three.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
S3 Bucket [app-media-prod] in us-east-1 (STANDARD) - Versioning: true
GCS Bucket [analytics-data] in europe-west1 (COLDLINE) - Retention: 90 days
Azure Blob [archive-store] in East US (ARCHIVE) - Access Tier: Hot
hints: CloudBucket constructor sets bucketName, region, storageClass.
Each sibling passes shared attributes to super() and formats output.
